t.3.62.1: Him, thus burning with grief, lamenting like one who has no protector, seized by a great bewilderment, utterly dejected and senseless…
t.3.62.2: Then Lakṣmaṇa, son of Sumitrā, having comforted him, after what seemed but a moment, addressed Rāma, pressing his feet.
t.3.62.3: By great austerity, O Rāma, and by great deeds as well, you were obtained by King Daśaratha, just as the nectar of immortality was obtained by the immortals.
t.3.62.5: If you, O Kākutstha, will not endure this sorrow that has come upon you, then what other person, ordinary and of little strength, will endure it?
t.3.62.4: Bound by your virtues, the lord of the earth, the king, attained the state of the gods because of separation from you, as was heard from Bharata.
t.3.62.6: For if you, stricken with grief, burn up the worlds with your fiery energy, where then, O tiger among men, will the afflicted people find peace?
t.3.62.7: This is the very nature of the world: Yayāti, the son of Nahuṣa, though he had attained the same world as Śakra, was touched by misfortune.
t.3.62.8: Among the great sages, Vasiṣṭha, who is our father's family priest, had a hundred sons born to him, and in a single day those same sons of his were slain.
t.3.62.9: And this goddess, who is the mother of the world and is revered by all people, this very earth is seen to tremble, O you who are true to your word.
t.3.62.10: And these two who are the eyes of the worlds, in whom everything is established, the mighty Āditya and Candra, have undergone eclipse.
t.3.62.11: O bull among men, even the mightiest beings and the gods, indeed all creatures and embodied beings, cannot escape the power of fate.
t.3.62.12: Even among the gods, beginning with Śakra, good fortune and misfortune are heard to prevail, O tiger among men; you should not be distressed.
t.3.62.13: Even though Vaidehī is lost, even though she has been carried off, O sinless one, you ought not to grieve, O hero, as some other ordinary man would.
t.3.62.14: For those like you, O Rāma, who always see the truth and whose outlook never yields to despair, do not grieve even in the very greatest hardships.
t.3.62.15: O best of men, reflect carefully and truly with your intellect, for the greatly wise, endowed with understanding, discern good and evil.
t.3.62.16: For deeds whose merits and faults remain unseen and which have not been firmly undertaken, the desired fruit does not come about without their actually being performed.
t.3.62.17: For in the past, O hero, it was you yourself who often instructed me; who indeed could instruct you, even if it were Bṛhaspati himself?
t.3.62.18: O greatly wise one, your understanding is hard to fathom even for the gods; I am awakening your knowledge, which has fallen asleep through grief.
t.3.62.19: O bull among the Ikṣvākus, considering divine and human prowess as well as your own valour, strive for the slaying of your enemies.
t.3.62.20: What would you gain by bringing about the destruction of everything, O bull among men? Rather, you should find out who that wicked enemy is and root out him alone.
